newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: New Zealand says Iranian trade ban not yet clear.
newsitem.headline: New Zealand says Iranian trade ban not yet clear.

text.p: Iran's embassy on Monday confirmed that Tehran had severed trade relations with New Zealand in the latest round of a diplomatic row, but New Zealand's foreign minister cast doubt on the development.
Don McKinnon said on Monday he was still not sure Iran had cut off trade relations, a move sparked by a German court ruling linking Iran to terrorism.

McKinnon issued a statement after meeting Iran's ambassador to Wellington, Mohammad Sazegara, on Monday evening that said: "The ambassador has told me he has not received any formal advice from Iran that a trade ban has been put in place against New Zealand. I am very pleased to receive that information."
Earlier on Monday, the Iranian embassy in Wellington had appeared to confirm that the trade ban, first reported by the official news agency IRNA on Saturday, was already in place.
It had also announced Sazegara would be recalled on Tuesday for consultation in a mirror of the action taken by New Zealand on Friday.

Hours earlier, the Iranian embassy here had issued a statement saying that Iran, through Construction Jihad Minister Gholamreza Forouzesh, "has ordered the suspension of all trade agreements with New Zealand parties until further notice".
Although it was not intially possible to clarify the exact status of the trade ban, both nation's diplomats used some conciliatory language and implied they wished to keep talking.

McKinnon said his talks with Sazegara had improved both sides' understanding of the others' point of view. He also reconfirmed New Zealand's intention to send its ambassador to Iran, Daniel Richards, back to Tehran by the end of this week.
Richards was recalled when New Zealand joined in a concerted international response to a German court ruling that Iran had ordered the 1992 murders of four Kurdish dissidents in Berlin.

The Iranian embassy on Monday criticised New Zealand for departing from a what it called "an independent position and vote" on international issues by joining this international action and taking part in "a political show against Iran".
However, the embassy statement also referred to the prospect of dialogue to smooth over relations later this week.
Sazegara would seek to meet his New Zealand counterpart Richards in a few days' time, it said.
The two hoped "to meet and discuss with Iranian authorities...with a view to normalising the relations between both countries on the basis of mutual respect", it added.
Since the row broke out at the weekend, some of New Zealand's primary exporters have expressed concerns about the effects of a full-scale ban on their agricultural produce trade.

The trade, mainly selling lamb, dairy produce and wool to Iran, is not large in overall terms, totalling an estimated NZ$170 million ($119 million) last year. But if suspended it could cause short-term problems, producers said.
However, at a news conference here earlier on Monday, International Trade Minister Lockwood Smith told reporters that New Zealand's main concerns were not financial.
Asked about the economic impact of a trade dispute, he said: "That's not the point... We have always had good relations with Iran and we want to get them back on a good footing."

His own analysis was that the talk of a trade ban might have stemmed from "some misunderstanding", and that in returning to Tehran, Sazegara would have the chance to make clear that New Zealand had no intention of curbing its trade links with Iran.
"New Zealand has never linked trade to these (political) issues... He (Sazegara) knows New Zealand is not planning any trade embargoes," Smith said.
